title: HTML Text and Headings
subtitle: How to make your app readable and professional
description: Learn how to structure text like a pro - headings hierarchy, paragraphs, bold vs strong, italic vs emphasis, line breaks, and text formatting that will make your final app look like a real product.

blocks.text: Welcome back - your app needs to speak clearly

Welcome back! In Lesson 1 you built the skeleton of your app. Now let's make it talk properly. Imagine you write a whole book without headings or paragraphs - nobody will read it. Same with apps. Today you will make your app readable, professional, and scannable.
Quick reminder: Open your lab - Home > Menu > Practical. You will need it today because text is all about seeing the difference. Run every code I give you there.
Headings are not about size - they are about structure
Most beginners think h1 to h6 are just for making text big or small. That's wrong and it will hurt your app's SEO and accessibility. Headings are about hierarchy - like chapters in a book.
h1 = Main title of entire page. Use only ONE per page. h2 = Major sections. h3 = Sub-sections inside h2. h4-h6 = Deeper levels. Google and screen readers use this hierarchy to understand your app.

blocks.text: Paragraphs and line breaks - small tags, big mistakes

p is for paragraph - a complete thought or idea. Browsers automatically add space before and after p. Many beginners use


to create paragraphs. That's unprofessional and breaks accessibility.
br means line break INSIDE same paragraph, like an address or poem. If it's a new idea, use new p, not br.

blocks.text: Bold vs Strong, Italic vs Emphasis - looks same, means different
This confuses everyone. <b> and <strong> both make text bold visually. <i> and <em> both make it italic. So why have 4 tags? Because meaning matters.

<b> = bold for style only, no extra importance. <strong> = bold PLUS this text is important, urgent, serious. Screen readers for blind users read <strong> with emphasis. <i> = italic for style like technical term. <em> = italic PLUS stress emphasis, like you would stress when speaking.

blocks.question: You need to warn users: 'Do not delete your database!' inside a paragraph. Which tag is semantically correct for the warning phrase and why?
options: Do not delete your database! because b makes it bold and bold is enough for warnings
Do not delete your database! because strong conveys semantic importance and urgency that assistive technologies announce, while b is purely presentational
Do not delete your database! because italic draws more attention than bold for warnings

Do not delete your database!

because warnings must be in separate paragraph not inside another paragraph
blocks.correctFeedback: Senior dev thinking! strong = importance, b = just visual. For warnings, meaning matters more than look.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Ask: Is this just visual styling or is it actually important/urgent content? Which tag conveys importance to screen readers?
blocks.reasoning: strong has semantic meaning of importance/urgency. b has no semantic importance, only visual bold.

blocks.question: Your page has h1 for site name, then you jump to h4 for a section title because you liked its small size. What breaks and what's the correct fix?
options: Nothing breaks visually, size is what matters so h4 is fine if you like the size - control size with CSS later but hierarchy must be logical h1->h2->h3
It's invalid HTML and page won't load - you must use h2 after h1, you cannot skip to h4 even with CSS
It breaks heading hierarchy for SEO and screen readers; fix by using h2 for section and controlling visual size with CSS, not by choosing h4 for its default size
It's correct to skip because h2 and h3 are deprecated and you should use only h1 and h4 in modern HTML5
blocks.correctFeedback: Exactly! Never choose heading level by size. Choose by structure, then style size with CSS.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Think: Headings are about structure not size. What does skipping levels do to SEO and accessibility?
blocks.reasoning: Heading levels represent document outline. Skipping breaks outline and confuses assistive tech and search engines.

blocks.text: Other powerful text tags real apps use daily
Beyond bold and italic, professional apps use small, mark, del, ins, sup, sub, blockquote, code tags daily. Let me show you how your final app will use them.

blocks.question: You want to show a price reduction: old price GH₵200 crossed out, new price GH₵150. Which is semantically correct for e-commerce and accessibility?
options:
Price: GH₵200 GH₵150

because del represents deleted/old price and ins represents inserted/new price, conveying change semantics
Price: GH₵200 GH₵150 with CSS line-through on first because bold is enough for prices

Price: GH₵200 GH₵150 with
between them because line break shows price change
Price: GH₵200 GH₵150 because mark highlights price changes
blocks.correctFeedback: Perfect e-commerce semantics! del/ins tells browsers and screen readers this is an edit/change, not just decoration.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Which tags convey meaning of deleted and inserted content? Not just visual effects.
blocks.reasoning: del and ins have semantic meaning of removal and insertion, ideal for price changes, document edits.

options:
H2O and E=mc2 and press Ctrl+S

because sub/sup represent subscript/superscript meaning and kbd represents keyboard input

blocks.correctFeedback: Outstanding! You used semantics correctly - sub for subscript chemistry, sup for superscript math, kbd for keyboard input.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Which tags convey actual meaning of subscript, superscript, and keyboard input vs just visual styling?
blocks.reasoning: sub, sup, kbd are semantic tags that convey specific meanings beyond visual appearance, improving accessibility and SEO.

blocks.text: You now write professional text - what's next?

You now know how to structure text like a pro developer - headings hierarchy that Google loves, paragraphs that screen readers understand, strong vs b, em vs i, and all the real-world text tags real apps use.

In Lesson 3: Links and Navigation, we will connect your pages together. Your single page will become a multi-page app with navigation menu, internal links, external links, and you will understand how every website navigation works. Go practice in Menu > Practical - try mixing h1, h2, strong, em, del, ins, sub, sup in your portfolio!
